Car Finance and Your Mortgage Application

PCP and HP are both credit commitments, and a mortgage lender counts them in full, not just what's left to pay. Here's what that means if you're buying a car and a house in the same year.

If you're buying a house in the next couple of years, the car decision is a mortgage decision too. Most people don't find that out until an underwriter tells them.

Why a car agreement costs you so much borrowing power

A car finance agreement is a monthly payment you've promised to make, and mortgage affordability is worked out by taking those promised payments away from the income you could otherwise put towards a mortgage. Roughly speaking, every £100 a month you're committed to elsewhere costs you £5,000 to £7,000 of borrowing power. A typical car agreement running at £300 to £400 a month is doing that several times over, so it can cost you somewhere between £15,000 and £28,000 of mortgage.

It isn't really a £300 payment. It's closer to twenty thousand pounds of house, give or take, for as long as the agreement runs. Put your own numbers through the affordability calculator with the car payment included, then again without it, and the gap between the two is usually sobering.

PCP and HP are not the same shape

With hire purchase, you pay off the whole cost of the car over the term. By the end you've paid for it and it's yours. The monthly payment is higher because you're actually buying the car.

With a personal contract purchase, you only pay off the depreciation each month, and a large payment is left at the end if you want to keep the car. That final payment is optional, and it's set at the outset based on what the car's expected to be worth when the agreement ends. Dealers call it the balloon. The monthly payment is lower because, in effect, you're paying to use the car rather than to own it. When the agreement ends, you can hand it back, pay the balloon, or roll into another agreement.

Two things follow from that, and they matter here:

  • PCP's lower monthly payment does less damage to your mortgage affordability than HP's higher one would, for the same car. If you need finance and you're applying for a mortgage too, that's a real argument for PCP, and it runs opposite to the usual advice, which is about total cost rather than affordability.
  • PCP usually costs more overall, and you end up owning nothing unless you also pay the balloon. Compare the totals properly with the PCP versus HP calculator, which shows the balloon rather than hiding it.

So the two goals genuinely pull against each other, and it's worth picking deliberately rather than letting a dealer pick for you.

The order of operations

If you're buying both a car and a house around the same time, the order you do them in matters more than almost anything else:

  1. Mortgage first, car second. Always, if you have any choice in the matter. Once your mortgage has completed, a new car agreement doesn't affect it at all. Do it the other way round, and the car eats into what house you can get.
  2. If the car really can't wait, keep the monthly payment as low as you can live with, and go in understanding you're trading house for car.
  3. Don't take out car finance between your mortgage application and completion. This is the mistake that costs people the most. Lenders check again before completion, and a new credit agreement showing up after a decision in principle can collapse the whole offer, often after you've already paid for a survey and legal work.

A decision in principle isn't a mortgage yet. The lender looks again before completion, and they do check. Between your application and getting the keys, it's best to change nothing: no new credit, no job change if you can avoid it, no large unexplained money moving through your account.

Existing agreement, mortgage coming: the options

  • Settle it. You have a statutory right to ask for a settlement figure. Clearing the agreement removes the monthly payment and gives you back the borrowing power it was costing you. It's the best option if you can afford it, and the figure you're quoted will include some early settlement interest, so it's worth estimating it here first.
  • Voluntary termination. Once you've paid half of the total amount payable under a regulated HP or PCP agreement, you have a statutory right under the Consumer Credit Act to end it and hand the car back, owing nothing further, as long as the car's in reasonable condition. That threshold is 50% of the total, and it's a genuine right that not enough people use. It isn't the same thing as voluntary surrender, which is a negotiated hand-back with the debt still owing, and the two get confused constantly.
  • Wait for the agreement to end, and time your mortgage application for after.
  • Do nothing, and accept the reduced figure the lender will offer you, once you've checked with the affordability calculator that it still buys what you need.

Handing a car back: the charges that appear at the end

Return charges are the surprise that catches most people out in car finance, and they're largely predictable if you know to look. Finance companies assess the car's condition against a published standard from the BVRLA, the trade body for vehicle leasing and rental. It's specific: it says how big a scratch is allowed to be, how much kerbing on an alloy wheel counts as acceptable, and what counts as damage rather than ordinary use. People call it the fair wear and tear standard.

There are two practical things you can do. Inspect the car against that standard a couple of months before the return date rather than on the day, which leaves you time to get small repairs done independently, usually for a fraction of what the finance company would charge. And check the excess mileage terms too: the per-mile rate looks small, but the totals often aren't.

The return damage checker walks through the standard item by item, so you can see where you stand before an inspector tells you.
